newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FOCUS - NZ loan rates ease despite strong homes mkt.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - NZ loan rates ease despite strong homes mkt.

text.p: HongkongBank on Friday opened the prospect of a new round of cuts in New Zealand home loan rates when it shaved its floating rate to 9.6 percent from 9.75.

The New Zealand unit of the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corp, often first to move rates because it funds off the local wholesale market, cited signs of a cooling of the housing market as the reason for its action.
But property and mortgage market players said they saw the current market providing limited justification for rate cuts and some saw the move more as a sign of competition among NZ banks.
HongkongBank made its move despite the key market indicator 90-day bank bill rate rising steadily over the last fortnight to nearly 8.0 percent from around 7.3 percent on March 13.
In political terms, any cooling in the housing market would bring a smile to face of Reserve Bank Governor Don Brash who has said rising home prices have become an inflationary factor.

In its June 1996 inflation forecast, the bank assumed that house prices would fall by 5.0 percent by the end of 1997. But latest figures from the Real Estate Institute show median prices in January stood 9.0 percent higher than a year ago.

While other lenders, and real estate agents, reported few signs of a significant slackening in demand in the market HongkongBank's Personal Banking Manager Alex Bentley insisted there was a slowing that was partly seasonal but also reflected signs of easing at the upper end of the market.
"I think we could see prices plateau through winter then drop," he told Reuters.
Rival lenders were more bullish.
"We've found demand has been very good," said ANZ Bank retail banking acting manager Rob Carthew, who added that ANZ had no plans to move its rate.
AMP's telephone bank Ergo, which has pressured other lenders since its entry into the market in 199!, reports no slowdown.
"We're certainly not, but I have heard from some other banks that the market is slowing," General Manager Graham Meyer said.
"In terms of slowing demand for mortgages, no, we're not seeing it. I think that is because we are a new player in the block and more and more people are trying us."

Meanwhile, the head of New Zealand's Real Estate Institute held another view. "There is fierce competition out there among the mortgage lenders. I believe that to be a very big factor (in pushing down rates)", its president Colin Brown said.

Ted Jewlett of Wellington firm Jewletts told Reuters, "There is no doubt that we are finding the volume of inquiry is not as strong as it has been over the last quarter, but the market is still going very, very well."
He said most houses were selling at the top end of the predicted range. Jewletts specialises in upmarket houses.

"Is the market slowing? No, I don't believe it is. There is a quietening effect starting to happen... but I don't believe the market is softening. I'm calling it a round market -- if you put the house on the market at an accurate price they are going out the door very quickly."
At his rival Leaders, another large Wellington player, sales manager Rob Garlick agreed. His firm's March sales were strongest for some months, he said.
"Prices continue to be firm and some ares continue to appreciate, particularly in the central city area."
